fetched_contents.text: Sexual offender recidivism revisited: a meta-analysis of recent treatment studies - Database of Abstracts of Reviews of Effects (DARE): Quality-assessed Reviews Authors' objectives To assess the effectiveness of different treatments for different types of sexual offender. Searching PsycLIT, PsycBOOKs, and reference lists of previously published reviews of outcome data on treatment for male sexual offenders, were searched from 1988 onwards for published studies not included in a previous review by Furby et al. (see Other Publications of Related Interest). Other restrictions, such as publication language, were not stated. Study selection Study designs of evaluations included in the review Published studies with 10 or more participants, a comparison or control group, and reported recidivism data were included. Limited information was provided on study designs included. The length of treatment varied from 4.5 to 60 months (mean 18.54 months; standard deviation, SD, 20.304) and follow-up from 1 to 20 years (mean 6.85 years; SD 5.95). Specific interventions included in the review The treatment modalities included behavioural, cognitive-behavioural, family therapy, group psychotherapy, hormonal (anti-androgen drug or castration), interpersonal, institutional programmes, individual psychotherapy, no-treatment comparison and medroxyprogesterone acetate. Participants included in the review Male sexual offenders, usually persons arrested for sexually aggressive behaviour including adolescents and men over the age of 17 years. Offences committed against women and children included rape, sexual assault, paedophilia, sodomy, exhibitionism and voyeurism. Studies were undertaken in out-patients and institutionalised care. Included studies were characterised by significant levels of participant exclusion from the analysis. Of the 80.9% (5,552 of 6,865 participants) excluded, the majority were associated with one study as a result of the non-matching of participants in treatment groups; removing this study left 35.8% of participants (620 of 1,733) excluded from the analysis. Excluded participants tended to be the most pathological participants, e.g. have extensive offences history, psychotic behaviour, organic brain syndrome, denied offences, or management problem in prison, or withdrew from the treatment programme. Outcomes assessed in the review Recidivism, i.e. additional sexually aggressive behaviour after a treatment period for participants who did and did not receive treatment, that led to official legal charges. Supporting evidence was provided by self-reports, or informal reports from agencies. How were decisions on the relevance of primary studies made? The author does not state how the papers were selected for the review, or how many of the reviewers performed the selection. Assessment of study quality The authors do not report the criteria used to assess validity, or how the validity assessment was performed. Methods of synthesis How were the studies combined? Individual effect size estimates were obtained for each study, to prevent any single study from disproportionately contributing to the results. The Pearson product-moment correlation was used as an estimate of effect size, with the correlation coefficients transformed to Fisher's z to normalise the distribution. Fisher's z scores were weighted for sample size, combined across studies and then divided by the sum of the sample size weightings for each study to produce a mean weighted Fisher's z. These were transformed to a correlation coefficient, then to Cohen's d. The fail-safe N was calculated, i.e. the number of studies averaging null results required to change the overall significance of the result from significant to insignificant. How were differences between studies investigated? Heterogeneity was assessed through a chi-squared analysis based on the sum of the weighted squared standard deviations of Fisher's Z scores. Results of the review Twelve studies with 1,313 patients. Limited information was provided on study designs. The recidivism rates for patients being treated were 19% (129 of 683 patients) compared to 27% (169 of 630 patients) for the comparison groups. The overall treatment effect (r) was 0.12 (d = 0.24), with a fail-safe (n) of 88 studies to bring the p value to insignificant. Treatment effect sizes were significantly heterogeneous with chi-squared of 70.91 (p<0.00001), thought to reflect differences in the base rates of recidivism across the studies, the differences in study design, variations in participant pathology and differences in treatment effects. Authors' conclusions This is an apparently robust result, although the authors suggest some caution in interpretation as only 12 studies were included and the analyses were affected by significant heterogeneity. In most studies over one third of participants were excluded on psychopathology, limiting the generalisability of the results. The results suggest the effect of treatment with sexual offenders is robust, albeit small, and that treatment is most effective with outpatient participants and when it consists of hormonal or cognitive-behavioural treatments. fetched_contents.text: Penile Plethysmography - an overview Chapters and Articles You might find these chapters and articles relevant to this topic. 3.7.1.1 Penile plethysmograph The penile plethysmograph is the most commonly used measure of deviant sexual arousal in males (McGrath et al., 2003); however, the research on the validity and reliability of this instrument is limited (Faniff & Becker, 2006). The device measures penile tumescence while the subject watches depictions of various appropriate and inappropriate sexual stimuli. The magnitude of the subject's erection is considered an indication of his sexual interest in that behavior (McGrath et al., 2003). Penile plethysmography techniques have been demonstrated to have internal consistency and test–retest reliability (Letourneau, 2002), although the methods of these validation studies have been criticized (Marshall, Anderson, et al., 1999; Marshall, Cripps, et al., 1999). Furthermore, the ethical, legal, and financial issues involved make the plethysmograph increasingly difficult to administer (Abel, Huffman, Warberg, & Holland, 1998). “PPG [penile plethysmography] is so cluttered with procedural inconsistencies and the failure to establish a standard protocol that it could not, in its present state, come close to being termed a norm-referenced test” (Laws, 2003, p. 93). Read full article URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1359178911000243 6.27.4.2.8 Physiological measures Physiological techniques have been used in the assessment of sexual function for many years, receiving impetus from the work of Masters and Johnson (1966, 1970). Measuring techniques are available for both male and female arousal. Penile plethysmography for the assessment of erection is widely used in research and can be used in clinical practice where needed and practicable (e.g., Wagner & Green, 1981; Wincze et al., 1988). The measure may be of either penile volume or penile circumference changes. Penile plethysmography has also been used to assess nocturnal erections in an attempt to distinguish psychogenic from organically caused impotence (Karacan, 1978). The injection of a chemical vasodilator, such as papa-verine, into one of the corpora cavernosa of the penis, is also used in the assessment of erectile disorder. If the patient develops a full erection following the injection, severe vascular insufficiency can be excluded as a cause of the problems (Brindley, 1983; Wagner, 1993). As for female arousal, the best established method is the photoplethysmography technique (Hoon, Wincze, & Hoon, 1976b), in which vasocongestion in the vaginal walls is measured with the help of a probe. Detailed discussions of these, and other laboratory techniques, for the assessment of sexual problems are provided by Bancroft (1989), Meisler and Carey (1990), McConaghy (1993), and Schiavi (1992). In a clinical setting, however, the use of physiological methods for routine assessment is not feasible. Also, the interpretation of their results in the clinical context is not always clear-cut (Bancroft, 1989; Conte, 1986). The “procedural” elements of PPG involve the presentation of sexual stimuli to a person and the concomitant measurement of changes in the circumference, length, or volume of the penis as a result of being exposed to the stimuli from a beginning point to an end point. The “technological” elements of PPG refer to the apparatus itself which records, translates and transmits these changes in penile responses during the procedure. A basic PPG apparatus is shown in Figure 3.1. However, both procedural and technological elements of the PPG continue to evoke controversy in both research and applied clinical settings. In this chapter, we will review both elements of PPG evaluations, with special consideration given to adolescent sexual offenders. fetched_contents.text: Emotion Goals: What Do Sexual Offenders Want to Feel? Abstract Sexual offenders typically experience more negative emotions and greater difficulties in regulating emotions than non-offenders. However, limited data exist on what sexual offenders want to feel (i.e., their emotion goals). Notably, emotion goals play a key role in emotion regulation and contribute to emotional experience. The present study tested whether sexual offenders (N = 31) reported higher scores for negative emotion goals and lower scores for positive emotion goals, compared with general offenders (N = 26) and non-offenders (N = 26). In addition, we tested whether sexual offenders differed from the other two groups in their perceived pleasantness and perceived utility of emotions. Sexual offenders reported greater scores for the emotion goal of sadness, and lower scores for the emotion goal of excitement, compared with both general offenders and non-offenders. State and trait levels of these emotions could not fully account for these differences. Furthermore, sexual offenders reported lower perceived pleasantness for sadness than general offenders and lower perceived pleasantness for excitement compared with both other groups. Finally, sexual offenders reported greater perceived utility of sadness than non-offenders. These novel findings and their implications for research and interventions are discussed in the context of sexual offenders’ emotional dysfunction. Keywords: sex offenders, general offenders, emotion goals, emotion regulation, excitement, sadness ---------------------------------------- The number of sexual offenses in several European countries has increased significantly since 2008 (EUROSTAT, 2019). A similar trend has been observed in the United States (Morgan & Kena, 2018). These crimes have important financial, social, and psychological costs. For example, in the United Kingdom, an analysis for the Home Office (Office for National Statistics, 2018) revealed that the financial impact of sexual assault alone is £2.5 billion per year, whereas in the United States, the cost goes up to $283,626 per victim (Heaton, 2010). Given its financial, psychological, and social ramifications, psychological research has long been interested in gaining a better understanding of the processes associated with sexual offending. Such understanding can provide valuable insights into the mechanisms that accompany the risk for sexual offending, as well as useful targets for interventions aimed at reducing (re)offending. A burgeoning literature has focused on the emotional functioning of sexual offenders. Such literature has shown that sexual offenders often report frequent and intense negative emotional experiences and experience difficulties in regulating emotions (Gillespie & Beech, 2016; Ward & Beech, 2016). Thus, these factors represent common objectives to address in the treatment of sexual offenders (Carter & Mann, 2016; Gillespie, Mitchell, Fisher, & Beech, 2012). In other words, existing research has shown that sexual offenders differ from non-offender controls in the way they feel and in the extent they are successful in regulating their emotions (Gillespie, Garofalo, & Velotti, 2018). What we do not know yet, however, is whether offenders are different in the direction in which they want to regulate their emotions—that is, in their emotion goals (i.e., what people want to feel). Importantly, this approach considers emotions not as automatic responses but as processes that can be changed depending on the superordinal standard or goal one aims to achieve (Tamir, 2016). Notably, endorsing an emotion goal as an emotion that an individual wants to feel more may indicate either a greater preference for that emotion or a lower aversion for that emotion. Because this study cannot speak to this nuance in distinguishing approach- and avoidance-emotion goals, we refer to emotion goals as “wanted” in relative terms. For example, one person may want to experience relatively more sadness than the other, even when both people want to experience only low levels of sadness. Indeed, such differences have been found when comparing certain clinical populations with control groups (López-Pérez, Ambrona, & Gummerum, 2018). Furthermore, although they reflected only relative and not absolute preferences, these differences nonetheless had important clinical implications (Millgram, Joorman, Huppert, & Tamir, 2015). Therefore, the present investigation tested whether sexual offenders differ from general offenders and non-offenders in their emotion goals. If such differences are found, they may add to our current understanding of emotional dysfunction in sexual offenders. Emotional Experiences and Emotion Regulation in Sexual Offenders Although there is considerable variability among individuals who commit sexual offenses, on average, sexual offenders have been characterized as experiencing negative emotions—including anger, fear, sadness, and general distress—more often and more intensely compared with other offender groups and non-offenders (Gillespie et al., 2012; Howells, Day, & Wright, 2004). Gillespie et al. (2012) and Howells et al. (2004) have reviewed the evidence for socio-affective difficulties that characterize individuals who commit sexual offenses, including a greater tendency to experience negative emotions compared with non-offenders. In addition, among sexual offenders, those reporting greater levels of negative emotions and difficulties regulating emotions tend to be more likely to recidivate after discharge (Gillespie et al., 2012). These negative emotional experiences are often triggered by problems in social relationships, typically related to the fear of intimacy and loneliness that characterizes sexual offenders (Martin & Tardif, 2015). Branch 3: methodological limitations and reliability concerns in offender research

The evidence here points to several overlapping limitations that weaken comparisons between self-report and physiological measures in sexual offender research. First, physiological measures such as penile plethysmography are not universally standardized, and their interpretation is difficult. The ScienceDirect overview states that penile plethysmography is the most commonly used measure of deviant sexual arousal in males, but its research on validity and reliability is limited, and it is vulnerable to faking [N3-F2]. It also notes that procedural inconsistencies and lack of a standard protocol make the measure “so cluttered with procedural inconsistencies ... that it could not, in its present state, come close to being termed a norm-referenced test” [N3-F2]. This matters because offender studies often rely on plethysmography to assess sexual interest, but its instability raises questions about whether responses reflect true arousal or other factors.

Second, physiological measures in real-world or offender settings are constrained by practical and ethical issues. The same overview says the ethical, legal, and financial issues involved make plethysmography increasingly difficult to administer [N3-F2]. This means many offender studies may be conducted in limited, institutionalized settings rather than ecologically valid ones, reducing generalizability. The evidence also notes that plethysmography may be used in clinical practice where needed and practicable, but its routine use is not feasible, and interpretation in clinical contexts is not always clear-cut [N3-F2]. That limitation is important because it suggests offender research may rely on a narrow subset of men in high-security or controlled settings, rather than representative samples.

Third, self-report measures face concerns about truthfulness and social pressure. The review of self-report measures in sexual offender research states that self-report is primarily used to assess personality traits, cognitions, and attitudes in offenders’ risk assessment, and that self-report data are often of questionable validity because many sex offenders engage in cognitive distortions [N4-R4]. A separate review on social desirability notes that SDR is a potential confounder when using self-report measures, especially in contexts with a high possibility of secondary gains or other incentives to present oneself favorably [N4-R2]. For offender research, this is especially relevant because self-report data are often collected in highly regulated, forensic settings where participants may feel pressure to conform to expectations, deny offending behavior, or downplay interest in deviant stimuli.

Fourth, study quality indicators in the evidence are mixed but notable. The meta-analysis on treatment for sexual offenders included only studies with 10 or more participants, a comparison or control group, and reported recidivism data, but it also excluded a large proportion of participants due to psychopathology, and it did not report the criteria used to assess validity [N2-F1]. That suggests many offender studies are small or selectively reported, which can distort comparisons between self-report and physiological outcomes. The evidence on physiological measures also emphasizes marked individual differences in responsivity in penile tumescence data [N3-R3], which implies that reliability may vary substantially across offenders even when the same procedure is used.

Overall, the strongest limitations are procedural inconsistency, limited validation, ethical/administrative burden, and the vulnerability of self-report to cognitive distortions and social desirability [N3-F2][N4-R2][N4-R4]. The quality evidence also shows that many offender studies are constrained by small samples, exclusions of pathological participants, and lack of standardized validity assessment [N2-F1]. Taken together, these limitations suggest that comparisons between self-report and physiological measures should be interpreted cautiously, because neither method alone produces a fully reliable picture of sexual interest in offenders.

The evidence supports multiple theoretical explanations for why self-reported and physiological measures of sexual interest may differ in sexual offender research. First, social desirability and secondary gains are major concerns. The review on social desirability notes that SDR is a potential confounder when using self-report measures, especially in contexts with a high possibility of secondary gains or other incentives to present oneself favorably [N4-R2]. For sexual offenders, this is especially plausible because self-report assessments are often conducted in forensic settings where participants may feel pressure to deny offending behavior, overreport prosocial traits, or underreport interest in deviant stimuli.

Second, denial and cognitive distortion are relevant. The review on self-report measures states that many sex offenders engage in cognitive distortions, which can affect truthfulness and self-report validity [N4-R4]. This means offenders may not accurately report their sexual interests because they believe such thoughts or behaviors are acceptable, justified, or not truly part of them. The same source also notes that self-report is used primarily to assess personality traits, cognitions, and attitudes in offenders’ risk assessment, which further suggests that self-report captures internal beliefs and attitudes rather than momentary physiological reactions [N2-R2].

Third, recall bias and measurement timing matter. The evidence on agreement between self-reported and genital measures of sexual arousal includes a meta-analysis that reviews research to quantify the extent of agreement between those two types of measures [N6-R1]. While the excerpt does not specify the direction of discrepancy, it indicates that self-report and genital measures are not perfectly aligned and that their relationship depends on study design and timing. The broader evidence on physiological measures also notes that responses can be influenced by the presentation of stimuli and the measurement context, because plethysmography involves watching depictions of various appropriate and inappropriate sexual stimuli and measuring physiological responses [N3-F2]. This suggests that self-report may reflect a broader, more reflective evaluation of interest, whereas physiology reflects a momentary reaction to specific stimuli, and the two may therefore diverge.

Fourth, differences in what the measures assess are central to interpretation. The review on forensic assessment notes that evaluated physiological techniques include penile plethysmography and pupillometry, while self-report measures include interviews, questionnaires, and card sorts [N5-R5]. The same overview says plethysmography is generally considered the sexual preference measure of choice, but it is vulnerable to faking [N3-F2]. This is important because physiological measures often aim to capture a more objective physiological correlate of interest, while self-report measures capture self-concept, belief, or memory of interest. The “Emotion Goals” study adds that sexual offenders differ in what they want to feel, reporting higher sadness and lower excitement than other groups [N5-F3], which supports the idea that self-report reflects a subjective, emotional goal system rather than a purely physiological state.

Finally, study design and measurement timing affect comparability. The meta-analysis on physiological arousal agreement states that the extent of agreement between self-reported and genital measures is what the review quantifies, implying that design choices such as stimulus type, measurement timing, and control conditions shape the results [N6-R1]. The evidence on plethysmography also notes that the measure is sensitive to procedural inconsistencies and lacks a standard protocol [N3-F2], which means comparisons across studies or offender groups can be unreliable if timing, stimuli, or recording procedures differ. This makes interpretation cautious: a discrepancy may reflect a real difference in interest, or it may reflect methodological variation, measurement timing, or context-dependent responding.

In sum, the evidence suggests that discrepancies arise from social desirability, denial, cognitive distortion, recall bias, and differences in what the measures capture [N4-R2][N4-R4][N5-F3][N6-R1]. The interpretation should therefore distinguish between genuine differences in interest or emotional experience and methodological or contextual differences in measurement [N3-F2][N5-R5].
